metadata.title: Boggs v. Boggs, 520 U.S. 833 (1997) (No. 96-79)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Boggs v. Boggs

Opinion filed: 1997-06-02

Docket No.: 96-79

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 45
• 117 S. Ct. 1754
• 520 U.S. 833
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 3396

Case holding summaries:
• QDRO provisions define scope of nonparticipant spouse's community property interest in pension plans
• preempting application of Louisiana's community property law which would have allowed first wife to make a testamentary transfer of her interest in participant's retirement benefits and survivor's annuity
• QDRO provisions define scope of nonparticipant spouse’s community property interest in pension plans
• conflict preemption requires state community property law to give way to ERISA, even though community property laws "implement policies and values lying within the traditional domain of the States."
• Congress intended to preempt nonbeneficiary nonparticipant interests in ERISA retirement plans
• the fact that a state law “implement[s] policies and values lying within the traditional domain of the States . . . inform[s] [a] preemption analysis”
• noting that Congress intended "to ensure a stream of income to surviving spouses"
• “A lifetime usufruct is the rough equivalent of a common-law life estate.”
• holding that ERISA preempted application of Louisiana community property law in state probate proceedings
• ERISA preempts state community property law that allowed testamentary transfer of an interest in a pension plan benefit
• "The principal object of the statute is to protect plan participants and beneficiaries."
• “In the face of [a] direct clash between state law and the provisions and objectives of ERISA, the state law cannot stand.”
• generally recognizing that QDROs confer beneficiary status upon certain nonparticipants and give those persons the same protection under ERISA as plan participants
• "We can begin, and in this case end, the analysis by simply asking if state law conflicts with the provisions of ERISA or operates to frustrate its objects."
• reviewing cases including In re Marriage of Campa, 89 Cal.App.3d 113, 152 Cal.Rptr. 362 (1979), dismissed for want of a substantial federal question, 444 U.S. 1028, 100 S.Ct. 696, 62 L.Ed.2d 664 (1980
• "We can begin, and in this case end, the analysis by simply asking if state law conflicts with the provisions of ERISA or operates to frustrate its objects."
• consider- ing congressional intent when analyzing qualified joint and survivor annuity benefits
• noting that only QDROs, not domestic relations orders in general, are saved from ERISA's general preemption provision and pension plan alienation provision
• noting that "QDRO's, unlike domestic relations orders in general, are ... exempt from ERISA's general preemption clause"
• rejecting the argu- ment that state law can apply when it affects “only the dispo- sition of plan proceeds after they have been disbursed by [the plan] and thus nothing is required of the plan”
• statutory restriction on class of permissible heirs constitutes taking
• Congress intended to preempt nonbeneficiary nonparticipant interests in ERISA retirement plans
• setting forth formula for calculating a former spouse's share of pension benefits
• "[The anti-alienation provision] reflects a considered congressional policy choice, a decision to safeguard a stream of income for pensioners . . . and their dependents . . ."
• "The several States, of course, have traditionally regulated the descent and distribution of estates"
• formula for calculating a former spouse's share of pension benefits
• state law is pre-empted when it falls within a field that Congress has sought to occupy
• first wife is entitled to reimbursement of her community property share of husband's pension contributions, but not from second, surviving wife; first wife is not entitled to share of second wife's survivor annuity
• to equalize allocation of community assets on termination, court may grant "cash or other property in lieu of an actual percentage of the pension payments"
• "[Dorothy's] spouse, or his estate, owes her an obligation to account for her share of the pension"
• decedent's IRA, which contained community property assets, could not be listed as an asset of his estate because he had designated a beneficiary; however, his estate would be deemed to contain the equivalent cash value
• federal statute stripping property owner of right to pass interest by descent or devise constitutes taking under Fifth Amendment
• States may not regulate activities that are protected or prohibited under National Labor Relations Act
• domestic relations law traditionally left to state regulation
• "ERISA is a comprehensive statute designed to promote the interests of employees and their beneficiaries in employee benefit plans"
• pre-empting state law and dis- cussing ERISA provisions with which it conflicts
• holding that ERISA preempted a Louisiana state law regulating community property when the insured sought to use a testamentary transfer to convey his interest in an ERISA plan
• holding that ERISA preempts “a state law allowing a nonparticipant spouse to transfer by testamentary instrument an interest in undistributed pension plan benefits”
• “In creating the QDRO mechanism Congress was careful to provide that the alternate payee, the ‘spouse, former spouse, child, or other dependent of a participant,’ is to be considered a plan beneficiary.”
• finding ERISA pre-emption of Louisiana state community property law
• stating that "one of REA's central purposes ... is to give enhanced protection to the spouse and dependent children in the event of divorce or separation, and in the event of death[,] the surviving spouse"
• explaining that states are not free to change ERISA's structure and balance
• explaining that Congress was careful "in creating the QDRO mechanism to allow the spouse, former spouse, child, or other dependent of a participant" to be a plan beneficiary
• all instructing that other domestic relations orders are expressly made subject to the anti-assignment provision and are, as a result, preempted
• noting that only QDROs, not domestic relations orders in general, are saved from ERISA's general preemption provision and pension plan alienation provision
• noting that "QDRO's, unlike domestic relations orders in gen- eral, are . . . exempt from ERISA's general preemption clause"
• holding that ERISA preempted a Louisiana state law regulating community property when the insured sought to use a testamentary transfer to convey his interest in an ERISA plan
• explaining that “ERISA is designed to ensure the proper administration of pension and welfare plans, both during the years of the employee’s active service and in his or her retirement years”
• analyzing whether state community property law frustrates federal interests in determining ERISA preemption
• finding that state law conflict with statute's provisions or objects was sufficient to resolve preemption question in favor of ERISA without resort to interpretation of statutory language
